note: DID YOU KNOW? facts bank. RESEARCH GATE APPLIED: every entry carries source(s), a verification date, and a chip. No entry ships from memory. Facts rot — recheck anything older than 12 months before reuse.
gate: source + second look + date + chip, or it does not ship

facts.body: When the English Base Set launched in January 1999, the artwork window sat flat against the yellow border — no shadow. A short way into the print run, Wizards of the Coast added a thin grey shadow down the right side and along the bottom of that window. Every card printed before that change lacks it; every card after has it. Collectors named the earlier ones "Shadowless" long afterward.
facts.why_it_matters: So you can sort a pile of Base Set cards in seconds: look at the right edge of the picture box. A clean edge means it came from those first few weeks, and those copies sell for meaningfully more than the ones printed for the two years that followed.

facts.hook: Base Set is the only main English expansion with no set symbol.
facts.body: Every other English main-series set stamps a small symbol beside the artwork. Base Set doesn't — so what identifies it is what's missing: no symbol at all, and a card number written out of 102.
facts.why_it_matters: So if you're digging through a bulk pile and a card has no little symbol beside the artwork and says something out of 102, you're holding a 1999 Base Set card — no card names required.
sources: Big Orbit Cards: Base Set identification guide

facts.hook: Base Set is 102 cards: 69 Pokémon, 26 Trainers, 7 Energy.
facts.body: The 16 holo rares are cards 1 through 16 — Charizard sits at 4/102. The set also established the layout the TCG still uses today: yellow border, HP top-right, and the weakness / resistance / retreat row along the bottom.
facts.why_it_matters: So the most famous card in the hobby, Charizard, sits at 4/102 purely because holo rares came first and C comes early in the alphabet. The hobby's landmark number is an accident of sorting.
sources: Bill's Archive: Base Set complete guide

facts.hook: There are two Pikachus in Base Set, and one is worth more.
facts.body: Pikachu 58/102 exists with red cheeks and with yellow cheeks. Red Cheeks appears only in the 1st Edition and Shadowless printings — every Unlimited Pikachu is Yellow Cheeks. Both PSA and CGC print the variant on the label inside the graded case, so it is officially recognised.
facts.why_it_matters: So if you own a Base Set Pikachu, check the cheeks. Red means it came from the earliest printings — worth more than the yellow-cheeked version everyone else has.
sources: Fanatics Collect: 1999 Base Set lot description (variant confirmed)

facts.hook: Nobody actually knows how many 1st Edition Base Set cards were printed.
facts.body: The figure repeated everywhere is 10,000 copies of each card. It has never been confirmed by Wizards of the Coast or The Pokémon Company. It circulates as community lore, not documented fact.
facts.why_it_matters: So the next time someone quotes a print-run number at you as though it settles an argument, remember that the most repeated figure in the hobby has no source behind it.
sources: Fanatics Collect auction description (states the figure has never been confirmed)
facts.note: Published as an unconfirmed-claim story, never as a print-run figure. Single-source; framed accordingly.

facts.hook: The very first Pokémon cards had no rarity symbol at all — and a printing mistake.
facts.body: Japan's original Expansion Pack from 1996 exists in two forms: with a rarity symbol in the corner, and without one. The symbol-less version is believed to be the earlier print run, because it carries errors that were later corrected — Venusaur was printed as Pokémon number 68 instead of 3. Collectors call it the No Rarity Base Set.
facts.why_it_matters: So if you ever handle a Japanese Base Set card, check the bottom-right corner of the art. Nothing there means you're holding one of the earliest Pokémon cards ever printed, mistakes and all.
sources: Bulbapedia: Base Set (TCG) — Japanese release section

facts.hook: There is a Base Set Charizard with a holo pattern that never went into production.
facts.body: CGC authenticated a 1999 Base Set Charizard test print that is missing pieces every normal card has — no Charmeleon in the evolution box, no flavour text under the art, no energy symbols. It also carries a shimmering foil pattern that appears on no regular Pokémon card. Test prints like it were usually never cut from the sheet, and when they were, they skipped the corner-rounding step, so the corners are square.
facts.why_it_matters: So square corners plus missing card elements is not damage or a fake — on rare occasions it is a factory test sheet that escaped, and graders treat it as its own category.
sources: CGC Trading Cards: certification article on the Base Set Charizard test print
facts.note: Single authoritative source (the grader who certified it). Framed as a documented certification, not a market claim.

facts.hook: There is a brand-new Base Set Charizard you cannot play with.
facts.body: The original 1999 Charizard artwork was reprinted for the Charizard & Ho-Oh deck in Pokémon Trading Card Game Classic. That reprint carries no regulation mark — the small letter modern cards use to show which seasons they are allowed in — so it cannot be used in sanctioned tournament play.
facts.why_it_matters: So if you are checking whether any modern card is tournament-eligible, look for a single small letter near the bottom of the card. No letter means it was never meant for competition, whatever the artwork says.

facts.hook: Charizard is card 4 of 102 because of the alphabet.
facts.body: The English Base Set was ordered by card type first, then by how rare the card was, then alphabetically by name. Among the holo rares that put Alakazam at 1, Blastoise at 2, Chansey at 3 — and Charizard at 4.
facts.why_it_matters: So the most recognisable number in the hobby, 4/102, is not a designation of importance. It is where the letter C landed.
sources: Bulbapedia: Base Set (TCG) — English release ordering
